content: Potassium acetate is a sterile, non-pyrogenic, concentrated solution of potassium acetate in water, approved by the FDA for the treatment of hypokalemia in patients with restricted or no oral intake. Common adverse reactions include potassium intoxication, which may manifest as paresthesias of the extremities, listlessness, mental confusion, weakness, heaviness of the legs, hypotension, cardiac arrhythmias, and heart block. Potassium acetate injection (USP, 40 mEq) is indicated as a source of potassium for addition to large-volume intravenous fluids to prevent or correct hypokalemia in patients unable to take potassium orally. It is also used as an additive for preparing specific intravenous fluid formulas when standard electrolyte or nutrient solutions are insufficient. This solution serves as an alternative to potassium chloride for providing potassium ions (K+) in intravenous infusion fluids. The injection must be diluted in a larger volume of fluid before intravenous administration. The dose and rate of administration depend on the individual needs of the patient. ECG and serum potassium levels should be monitored to guide dosage. Using aseptic technique, the contents of one or more vials may be added to other intravenous fluids to achieve the desired milliequivalents (mEq) of potassium (K+) and acetate (CH3COO−). The maximum infusion rate should not exceed 1 mEq/kg/hr. Parenteral drug products should be inspected visually for particulate matter and discoloration prior to administration. Potassium acetate administration is contraindicated in patients with severe renal insufficiency, adrenal insufficiency, or conditions associated with hyperkalemia. It must be diluted before use, and potassium-containing solutions should be infused slowly to avoid potassium intoxication. Continuous or serial ECG monitoring is recommended during potassium replacement therapy, as serum potassium levels may not reliably indicate tissue potassium levels. Caution is advised when using potassium acetate in patients with hyperkalemia, severe renal failure, or conditions of potassium retention. In patients with diminished renal function, potassium-containing solutions may lead to potassium retention. Acetate-containing solutions should be used cautiously in patients with metabolic or respiratory alkalosis or severe hepatic insufficiency. This product contains aluminum, which may be toxic, particularly in patients with impaired kidney function or premature neonates. Prolonged parenteral administration of aluminum at levels greater than 4 to 5 mcg/kg/day may lead to central nervous system and bone toxicity. Potassium acetate should not be administered unless the solution is clear and the seal is intact. Unused portions should be discarded. High plasma potassium concentrations can cause cardiac depression, arrhythmias, or arrest. Caution is necessary in patients with cardiac disease, particularly those on digitalis therapy or with renal disease. Excess administration of acetate may result in metabolic alkalosis. Adverse reactions include the potential for potassium intoxication, with symptoms such as paresthesias, flaccid paralysis, listlessness, mental confusion, weakness, heaviness of the legs, hypotension, cardiac arrhythmias, heart block, ECG abnormalities (e.g., disappearance of P waves, widening of the QRS complex), and cardiac arrest. In the event of overdose, discontinue potassium acetate infusion immediately and initiate corrective therapy to reduce elevated serum potassium levels and restore acid-base balance if necessary. Potassium acetate plays a critical role in fluid and electrolyte balance as the principal cation of intracellular fluid. Acetate serves as an alternative source of bicarbonate (HCO3−) through metabolic conversion in the liver, even in severe liver disease. Potassium acetate injection (USP, 40 mEq) is supplied in 20 mL single-dose vials and should be stored at 20 to 25°C (68 to 77°F).
